item.title: BBC to close three TV, radio channels amid cost pressures
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21
This photo taken on Oct. 20, 2026 shows an exterior view of the Broadcasting House of the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) in London, Britain. The BBC reported Tuesday it will close its BBC Three and BBC Scotland television channels in the spring, as the corporation continues to make 500 million pounds (669 million U.S. dollars) of savings over two years. (Xinhua/Li Mangmang) LONDON, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- The BBC reported Tuesday it will close its BBC Three and BBC Scotland television channels in the spring, as the corporation continues to make 500 million pounds (669 million U.S. dollars) of savings over two years. Both services will become online-only, which means that they will continue to produce and host some content on iPlayer, without the need to fill a terrestrial TV schedule, according to the report. The BBC also announced that it will close Radio 4 Extra, which largely airs speech programs from the BBC's archive, including comedy, drama and documentaries. The decision was made in response to "immediate cost pressures," said BBC Director-General Matt Brittin, adding that "we all know that means tough choices." "Against the backdrop of significant financial challenges, we must focus our resources where they will have the greatest impact for audiences," said Director of BBC Scotland Hayley Valentine. ■ This photo taken on Oct. 20, 2026 shows an exterior view of the Broadcasting House of the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) in London, Britain. item.title: Chinese premier eyes further alignment of development strategies with Tajikistan, higher-quality SCO development with all parties
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21
DUSHANBE, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- During a packed three-day visit of high-level engagements in Dushanbe, Chinese Premier Li Qiang said China is willing to deeply align its development strategies with Tajikistan and advance high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, and work with all parties to promote higher-quality development of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO). Li arrived here Sunday for an official visit and the 25th meeting of the Council of Heads of Government (Prime Ministers) of Member States of the SCO in Tajikistan. In his meeting with Tajik President Emomali Rahmon, Li said that China stands ready to broaden bilateral trade with Tajikistan, strengthen cooperation in infrastructure, green minerals, connectivity and other fields, and expand cooperation in emerging industries such as the digital economy and artificial intelligence to jointly build new drivers of economic growth. China will import more high-quality goods from Tajikistan, encourage Chinese enterprises to invest and start businesses in Tajikistan, and hopes that Tajikistan will continue to provide a favorable business environment for enterprises, Li said during his talks with Tajik Prime Minister Kokhir Rasulzoda. Both sides should expand exchanges and cooperation in areas such as culture, education, health, sports and local-level fields to enhance the sense of gain of the people of both countries, said Li, noting that the two countries should continue to deepen law enforcement and security cooperation to foster a stable and secure environment for personnel exchanges between the two sides. This year, China begins the implementation of its 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), and Tajikistan is also advancing its National Development Strategy for the period up to 2030, Chinese President Xi Jinping said in his talks with Rahmon in May this year, adding that the two sides should focus on high-quality Belt and Road cooperation and further align their development strategies. Now the two countries are seeking to enhance the alignment and cooperation across various fields to support the pursuit of their respective development goals. Data show that China is Tajikistan's largest trading partner. In 2025, bilateral trade exceeded 30.8 billion yuan (about 4.5 billion U.S. dollars), up 12.5 percent year on year. During Li's visit, the two sides witnessed the signing of multiple documents covering infrastructure development, education, anti-corruption and standardized cooperation. Guzel Maitdinova, director of the Center for Geopolitical Studies at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University, told Xinhua that the interaction between the two countries is gradually evolving into a multi-level system of cooperation -- encompassing political, economic, infrastructural, technological, and humanitarian spheres -- that is closely linked to the development of the SCO, China's Belt and Road Initiative, and broader regional processes in central Eurasia. In his speech at the 25th meeting of the Council of Heads of Government (Prime Ministers) of Member States of the SCO, Li said that all parties need to build greater consensus both on the level of underlying principles, including vision, philosophy and thinking, and the level of practical approaches, including operations and implementation, so as to shoulder its historic responsibility and take the initiative in steering the course of history. Li said that the SCO should strengthen economic and trade cooperation and promote regional economic integration by leveraging the complementary strengths of its members, build a stable and resilient system of international transport corridors, and safeguard the stability and smooth functioning of global industrial and supply chains. The SCO should also seek common interests amid differences in countries' concerns and work together to uphold world peace and stability, while promoting harmony and coexistence amid cultural differences, he added. This year marks the 25th anniversary of the founding of the SCO. Over the past 25 years, it has shown that countries with different political systems, development paths and civilizations can pursue cooperation together. "The SCO's international significance is therefore determined not only by its geographical reach or the combined potential of its member states, but also by its ability to translate political agreements into functioning mechanisms for security, economic cooperation, and diplomatic coordination," said Maitdinova. Amid profound changes in the international landscape, the international role of the SCO is acquiring new dimensions. The organization is becoming not only a platform for regional dialogue and security coordination, but also a mechanism for reconciling the interests of states within an emerging multipolar world order, the expert added. China stands ready to work hand in hand with all member states to enhance the organization's operational efficiency, strengthen and consolidate cooperation projects, and play a leading and exemplary role in advancing the SCO's high-quality development, implementing the four global initiatives proposed by President Xi, and building a community with a shared future for humanity, Li said. China is ready to work with all parties to strengthen coordination and complete, as soon as possible, the institutional frameworks and rules for the four security centers, said Li, noting that China is also willing to sponsor 1,000 medical professionals from SCO countries to come to China for further training. China, as one of the founding members of the SCO, has consistently expanded the organization's cooperation agenda and contributed to its development, SCO Deputy Secretary-General Ahmad Saidmurodzoda said in an earlier interview with Xinhua. ■

item.title: 90 years after Liangzhu's discovery, a lost city and a civilization brought back to life
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20
HANGZHOU, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- Across the landscape, golden rice is ready for harvest in the fields about an hour's drive northwest of downtown Hangzhou, in east China's Zhejiang Province. Reeds sway in the breeze. An egret skims the water, leaving ripples in its wake. Xu Rushui, 70, tends the rice. The farmer, the fields and, in the distance, statues depicting scenes from everyday life in ancient Liangzhu evoke generations of people who worked this land -- and a history that continues to shape the region today. The scene is part of the Archaeological Ruins of Liangzhu City, a UNESCO World Heritage site dating to between 5,300 and 4,300 years ago. Archaeologists believe it was a center of power and belief for an early regional state in late Neolithic China, in the lower reaches of the Yangtze River. Liangzhu took its place alongside the early civilizations of ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley. New discoveries continue to reveal how this ancient city was built and how its people lived. Wang Ningyuan, a researcher at the Zhejiang Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology, discussed the latest findings on the sidelines of the fourth Liangzhu Forum, which was held from Oct. 18 to 20 in Hangzhou. Archaeologists have reconstructed three prehistoric buildings east of a royal cemetery based on postholes uncovered during excavations, Wang said. The largest is oval-shaped. The buildings may offer clues to how early rulers were honored in death. Further excavations could help test that hypothesis and reveal more about how the structures were used, he said. The year 2026 marks 90 years since the Liangzhu ruins were first discovered. The forum named after the site made its debut in 2023 and has since grown into a major venue for international dialogue on cultural heritage. This year's edition, held under the theme "Bridging the Past and the Future: Safeguarding Cultural Heritage for Our Times," featured discussions ranging from early civilizations to the archaeology of ancient cities, with new research findings released. Nayef Al-Fayez, UNESCO Assistant Director-General for Culture, said in a video speech at the opening ceremony that Hangzhou, whose region is home to a number of World Heritage properties, including the Liangzhu site, reflects 5,000 years of advanced urban planning and cultural exchange. "It reminds us of the value of the heritage and the importance of safeguarding it for future generations," he said. A CITY BUILT ON WATER, RICE AND JADE The ruins take their name from the nearby town of Liangzhu, which literally means "beautiful islets amid the waters." Built on low-lying land once crisscrossed by waterways, the ancient city comprised a palace complex, an inner city and an outer city, along with an extensive water-management system and settlements spread across the surrounding landscape. Across this broader archaeological site, researchers have uncovered evidence of palaces, altars, elite burial grounds and craft workshops. Waterways were integral to daily life in the ancient city. Of its nine gates, one opened onto land, while the other eight connected the city's waterways with those outside. People traveled in dugout canoes carved from tree trunks and on rafts made by binding bamboo poles. Rice farming formed the base of the economy. Archaeological evidence suggests that settlements specialized in different forms of production, including jade working and stone-tool making. Liangzhu's society was marked by pronounced social stratification, specialized production and a shared system of religious beliefs, said Fang Xiangming, director of the Zhejiang Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology. Its trove of jade artifacts offers a particularly revealing window into this social order. Among them is the famed "king of jade cong," a tubular object with a square exterior and a circular interior, carved with distinctive divine-human and animal motifs. Jade cong artifacts reflected the ancient people's understanding of the cosmos, embodied their shared beliefs and left a lasting imprint on later generations, said Xu Tianjin, director of the Liangzhu Museum. The monumental engineering works of Liangzhu offer another window into the organization of this ancient society. To the northwest of the city, inhabitants built an elaborate network of dams and levees to help manage floods, irrigate farmland and facilitate transportation. It ranks among the oldest large-scale hydraulic systems identified to date in China. According to Wang, a leading expert on the site's ancient waterworks, the system created a reservoir with a total capacity of about 46 million cubic meters. That is roughly four times the capacity of Hangzhou's West Lake, or the equivalent of 18,400 Olympic-size swimming pools. Estimates suggest that building the ancient city and its surrounding waterworks required the movement of a combined 10.05 million cubic meters of earth and stone, roughly twice the estimated volume involved in constructing the Pyramids of Giza in Egypt. The scale of these projects points to a society with sophisticated planning capabilities and the ability to mobilize large numbers of people for collective undertakings, Wang said. WHAT MAKES A CIVILIZATION? Unlike many ancient societies, Liangzhu left behind no written records -- not even legends. Its history has been pieced together largely through archaeological excavations and the material remains unearthed in the process. For centuries, writing systems, metallurgy and cities have often been treated as criteria for civilization in Western accounts of early societies. Liangzhu has helped broaden that perspective, according to Wang Wei, a senior member of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. In simple terms, he said, three key developments mark the emergence of a civilized society: cities arising as productivity advances and population grows; distinct social classes taking shape as the division of labor deepens and society becomes more differentiated; and the concentration of power paving the way for kingship and the state. The Liangzhu ruins have provided material evidence for Chinese civilization spanning more than 5,000 years. The site's inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2019 brought wider international attention to the achievements of China's early civilization. Research under a national project led by Wang Wei during the first two decades of this century uncovered evidence that the origins of Chinese civilization can be traced to multiple regions. Around 5,800 years ago, early signs of civilization were emerging not only along the Yangtze River, where Liangzhu is located, but also in the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River and the Xiliao River basin. A PAST THAT LIVES IN THE PRESENT The legacy of Liangzhu lives on not only in artifacts excavated and housed in museums, but also in the daily lives of people today. For farmer Xu Rushui, who works the park's rice fields with three other farmers across a combined area of more than 880 mu (around 59 hectares), the fields are more than just scenery. They remain a source of income for his family. Restrictions on chemical inputs, combined with the area's cultural heritage, have given the rice a distinctive identity. What was once simply a crop now has a story to tell -- one that helps it stand out in the market. "Five thousand years ago, people planted rice by hand. Now we have machines, and visitors come to see the fields," said Xu. "A lot has changed, but rice is still part of our lives. We still depend on this land to make a living." Beyond the villages, Liangzhu is helping reshape the wider region. A cultural corridor spanning hundreds of square kilometers links the archaeological site with nearby heritage sites, cultural institutions and the surrounding hills, waterways, villages and woodlands. A new generation of creators and entrepreneurs is emerging here. Programmers and designers in their 20s mingle with investors and seasoned engineers from major tech companies, bringing fresh ideas to this ancient land. Master Qi (a pseudonym), a product manager who moved from Beijing, started by hosting informal discussions in his living room. Those gatherings have since grown into a lively hub where AI creators share projects, exchange ideas and find collaborators. "You get the openness and quiet of the countryside, along with the conveniences of city life," he said. "The low-rise buildings, the space between them, the cafes where people talk about AI, and the remote workers, indie developers and content creators you see everywhere -- it all fuels my creativity." Liangzhu is also drawing an increasingly international crowd. It has hosted exchanges with heritage professionals involved in preserving historical sites in Toledo, Spain, and Rome, Italy. Dorian Fuller, a fellow of the British Academy and professor at the Institute of Archaeology, University College London, was in Hangzhou to attend the fourth Liangzhu Forum. On Sunday, the archaeologist tried a pair of AI glasses at the Liangzhu Museum -- a device that identifies exhibits in the wearer's field of view, provides explanations and answers visitors' follow-up questions. "I can see how it would be appealing maybe to the younger generation and people who are new to archaeology and are kind of learning about this stuff for the first time," Fuller said. The museum's augmented reality (AR) glasses also allow visitors to watch a virtual jade cong float out of its case and rotate digitally in midair, revealing intricate carvings from every angle without touching the original. Yet much remains unknown. Wang Ningyuan, who has worked at Liangzhu since 2000, said archaeologists have excavated just 60,000 square meters within a 100-square-kilometer area, leaving vast stretches untouched. Phytolith analysis, for example, has found no evidence of rice paddies in the outer city area, suggesting that grain may have come from beyond the city. If so, how was it grown, transported and brought to the people who lived there? Nine decades after its discovery, Liangzhu is still yielding its secrets. ■

item.title: Fueling developing world's energy transition, China takes green energy global
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20
An aerial drone photo taken on Aug. 24, 2022 shows a view of the 330-megawatt Phu My Solar Power Plant in Gia Lai province in Vietnam. (Xinhua) BEIJING, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- As developing countries seek pathways to energy transition, China's renewable energy supply chains, engineering capabilities and operational expertise are opening up new possibilities for renewable energy development. From solar farms in Southeast Asia to off-grid systems in rural Africa, China's clean energy projects are expanding electricity access, creating jobs and building local skills. In 2021, China pledged to stop building new coal-fired power plants overseas. Green energy has since become a focus of cooperation with Belt and Road partner countries, with Chinese companies involved in solar, wind and hydropower projects that support local energy transitions. SOLAR PARTNERSHIP DRIVES LOW-CARBON GROWTH Across Southeast Asia, Chinese-built renewable energy projects are helping meet rising power demand and cut emissions. In Indonesia's West Java province, the 100-megawatt Karawang photovoltaic project, constructed by China Electric Power Construction Group Hubei Engineering Co., Ltd., began operation in 2024. It supplies clean electricity to the industrial park in Karawang, cutting annual carbon dioxide emissions by 19,800 tons and saving about 8,800 tons of standard coal. The project has also strengthened local expertise. During construction, the Chinese team trained more than 300 Indonesian workers, helping build a local workforce capable of independently installing solar systems. In Vietnam, PowerChina Jiangxi Electric Power Engineering Co., Ltd. built the 330-megawatt Phu My Solar Power Plant in Gia Lai province. Engineers adapted equipment and mounting structures to withstand coastal salt corrosion, high temperatures and typhoons. The plant generates about 520 million kilowatt-hours annually, reducing carbon dioxide emissions by roughly 400,000 tons a year. Construction has created more than 2,000 local jobs, while training helped develop skills in renewable energy operations and maintenance. Beyond solar energy, China-Vietnam energy cooperation now spans wind, hydropower and waste-to-energy, broadening the two countries' clean energy partnership. CLEAN POWER CUTS ENERGY COSTS In Pakistan, Chinese solar products and technology are helping diversify an energy mix long reliant on thermal power. As the South Asian country grapples with high electricity costs and unreliable supply, expanding solar capacity has brought clean power to millions of households. Chinese companies have also introduced flexible installment plans to make solar systems more affordable, helping families lower electricity bills. The under-construction China-built Mohmand Hydropower Project in Pakistan is expected to generate 2.86 billion kilowatt-hours annually and has created more than 5,000 local jobs, strengthening Pakistan's construction capabilities. China's green energy projects also support economic development in partner countries. Construction creates local jobs and trains skilled workers, while solar panels and energy storage systems help grow supply chains in infrastructure, logistics and maintenance. With no fuel costs, wind and solar power offer more predictable long-term generation costs than fossil fuels, helping reduce electricity bills for households and businesses while providing affordable power for local industries. OFF-GRID SOLAR EXPANDS ENERGY ACCESS Across Africa's vast landscapes, dispersed populations and complex terrain have made conventional grid expansion costly and difficult. Many rural and pastoral communities remain without reliable electricity. China has responded with lightweight, easy-to-install off-grid solar and storage systems. Operating independently of main grids, they deliver stable power and help close "the last mile" of energy access. In Kenya's pastoral areas, remote villages and refugee camps, Chinese solar equipment has replaced costly, polluting diesel generators. It now supports daily life, local festivals and small businesses. Solar lighting has extended school hours in rural areas, while photovoltaic irrigation pumps have cut farming costs and increased crop yields by about 30 percent in some cases. Clean, stable and affordable green power is doing more than lighting homes. It is strengthening education, agriculture and small-scale economies, creating steadier income for local people. China's overseas energy cooperation has shifted from coal-fired projects to green energy partnerships. By combining project construction with technology transfer and talent training, it helps partner countries build self-sustaining green energy systems. As high-quality Belt and Road cooperation deepens, China is helping developing countries turn wind, solar and water resources into drivers of growth, improving livelihoods while advancing a shared low-carbon future. ■ A technician works at the 330-megawatt Phu My Solar Power Plant in Gia Lai province in Vietnam, Oct. 13, 2026. item.title: China firmly opposes U.S. sanctions on Chinese AI companies: commerce ministry
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20
BEIJING, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Commerce on Tuesday voiced strong dissatisfaction and resolute opposition to the latest U.S. move, which ordered its federal civilian agencies to stop using artificial intelligence (AI) products and services from Chinese companies. China adheres to placing equal emphasis on development and security, ensuring that AI remains safe, controllable, and reliable, a ministry spokesperson said. Chinese AI companies have consistently been committed to providing safe and reliable services for global users while abiding by the laws of host countries, earning widespread recognition worldwide. The U.S. side has taken discriminatory restrictive measures against Chinese AI companies for so-called national security concerns, the spokesperson stressed, saying the U.S. move is a typical act of overstretching the concept of national security and abusing administrative means to suppress Chinese enterprises. It severely harms the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies, undermines a fair competitive market environment, and disrupts normal commercial cooperation between China and the U.S. in the AI sector, the spokesperson said. Meanwhile, the spokesperson firmly opposed the recent U.S. sanctions on Chinese companies over the so-called issue of "theft of trade secrets," saying this malicious act has seriously harmed their legitimate rights and interests. The rapid development of Chinese AI companies has been driven by long-term commitment to basic research and sustained investment in innovation, which serves the interests of China, the United States and the rest of the world, the spokesperson noted. China urges the U.S. side to immediately correct its wrong practices, stop the unreasonable suppression of Chinese companies, and revoke relevant discriminatory restrictive measures, and hopes the United States will earnestly implement the important consensus reached by the two heads of state and make good use of the China-U.S. AI dialogue mechanism. China will closely monitor developments and take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard the country's and its enterprises' legitimate rights and interests, the spokesperson added. ■

item.title: China's top economic planner vows more efforts to expand domestic demand
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20
BEIJING, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's top economic planner said Tuesday it will work with relevant departments to expand domestic demand with greater force and more effective measures in an effort to consolidate the foundation and momentum for steady economic recovery. The National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) revealed this at a press conference on Tuesday following the release of the latest economic data on Monday, which showed the world's second-largest economy pressed ahead against pressures with a 4.6-percent economic growth in the first three quarters of 2026. Commenting on the economic performance, NDRC official Zuo Gang said the economy, in the face of intensifying global geopolitical conflicts and frequent natural disasters, has demonstrated strong resilience and vitality with new growth drivers and improved structure. Due to challenges such as the deepening impact of external shocks, an imbalance of strong supply and weak demand at home, and pronounced sectoral divergence, further measures will be taken to rev up the economy, according to the official. "The NDRC will work with relevant departments to promptly introduce and implement incremental policies and promote synergy between existing and incremental policies with a view to achieving a good start for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030)," Zuo said. China has targeted 2026 growth at 4.5 to 5 percent and will strive for better in practice. BOOSTING CONSUMPTION More efforts will be made to vigorously boost consumption, Zuo said. Authorities will raise the share of public service spending in fiscal expenditure, strengthen inclusive policies that reach consumers directly, and promote the expansion and upgrading of goods consumption, including new energy vehicles and smart products, Zuo said. The push comes as consumption shows signs of steady improvement. Total retail sales of goods and services rose 2.6 percent year-on-year in the first three quarters of 2026, with retail sales of services growing faster than goods and new forms of consumption continuing to emerge, official data showed. Final consumption expenditure contributed more to overall economic growth in the January-September period. Chinese authorities have recently introduced a raft of measures aimed at boosting domestic demand, including offering interest subsidies for the housing loans of eligible homebuyers to help reduce home-buying costs and better unlock housing demand. Through ultra-long special treasury bond issuance, 250 billion yuan (about 37.2 billion U.S. dollars) has been raised to support consumer goods trade-in programs, and 200 billion yuan to support large-scale equipment upgrades this year. Furthermore, 50 billion yuan was earmarked for the establishment of a special fiscal-financial coordination fund to boost domestic demand. In addition to measures already announced, including lowering interest rate for pledged supplementary lending and increasing relending quotas to support sci-tech innovation and technological upgrades, "we will introduce new incremental policies in a timely manner as needed to ensure that the economy operates within an appropriate range," Zuo said. PROMOTING INVESTMENT Zuo said China will invest in both physical assets and human capital to expand effective investment. Specifically, the NDRC will push for the implementation of the 109 major projects outlined in the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) and the "six networks" initiative, covering water, power, computing, communications, urban underground pipelines and logistics networks, Zuo said. Ultra-long special treasury bond funds will be deployed more effectively, and the new policy-based financial instruments will be used at a faster pace, Zuo said, also vowing stronger support for social welfare, technology innovation, industrial upgrading and security resilience. Zuo revealed plans to energize private investment by introducing private capital into major nuclear power, hydropower, and water conservancy projects. He also identified the optimization of computing power facility layouts and the renovation and upgrading of aging reservoirs as additional investment priorities. China's investment is undergoing a profound shift in emphasis from traditional sectors to emerging ones, analysts said, noting that artificial intelligence and new infrastructure will serve as key engines for the next round of effective investment. Official data showed the country's investment in innovation-driven sectors held up well in the first three quarters of 2026, even as overall fixed-asset investment continued to contract. Investment in intellectual property products rose 9.3 percent year-on-year in the January-September period, while investment in high-tech industries grew 4.9 percent. Investment will increasingly serve the development of new quality productive forces and the building of a modern industrial system, with the ultimate results felt in expanded employment, rising incomes and improved living standards, said Liu Yuanchun, president of Shanghai University of Finance and Economics. ■

item.title: Enduring Long March spirit boosts China's drive for national rejuvenation
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20
BEIJING, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- The enduring spirit of the historic Long March continues to boost China's drive for national rejuvenation, inspiring the Chinese people to overcome hardships and secure new achievements in Chinese modernization. This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, a remarkable revolutionary feat achieved under the leadership of the Communist Party of China (CPC). The Long March constitutes a monumental chapter in the historical journey toward the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. From October 1934 to October 1936, the CPC-led Red Army soldiers broke through the encirclement of Kuomintang forces, crossed more than 10 provinces, and braved raging rivers, snow-capped mountains and treacherous grasslands before finally completing their epic military maneuver. The Long March victory marked a major turning point from setbacks to victory for the CPC and the Chinese revolution, and ushered in a new phase in the CPC's struggle for national independence and the people's liberation. The Long March spirit features firm revolutionary ideals and convictions, dauntless courage and sacrifices, independence and truth-seeking, strict discipline and unity, and close ties with the people. This spirit has been deeply embedded in the identity of the Chinese nation. The CPC has led the Chinese people through revolution, socialist construction and reform. In the new era, China has secured historic achievements and seen historic changes in the cause of the Party and the country, while withstanding risks, challenges, and trials in some domains. Most notably, the country, with a population of over 1.4 billion, eradicated millennia-old absolute poverty and completed the building of a moderately prosperous society in all respects. Chinese modernization is a pioneering and arduous undertaking. The spirit of struggle is essential to breaking new ground and securing new victories. Externally, China faces containment and suppression of its development, as well as rising unilateralism and protectionism. Domestically, it needs to resolve deep-seated problems regarding reform, development and stability, pursue high-quality development, enhance sci-tech self-reliance, and promote common prosperity. China is on a new journey to build a modern socialist country in all respects. On the new Long March, China stands ready to withstand high winds, choppy waters, and even dangerous storms, and will resolutely safeguard its national sovereignty, security, and development interests, in a bid to write a new chapter in sustaining the miracles of rapid economic growth and long-term social stability. As the victory of the Long March proved, the people possess boundless wisdom and strength. The CPC upholds its fundamental purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly and follows a people-centered development philosophy. Realizing national rejuvenation also relies on the people's support, wisdom and strength. The leadership of the CPC offers a fundamental guarantee for achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Only by unswervingly upholding the leadership of the CPC can Chinese modernization have a bright future. In the new era, the CPC has strengthened Party leadership in all respects and made significant advances in exercising full and rigorous Party self-governance. As the largest governing party in the world, the CPC is leading the Chinese people of all ethnic groups in a concerted effort to advance toward national rejuvenation. During the 2026-2030 period, China aims to make decisive progress toward basically realizing socialist modernization by 2035. The Long March spirit will always serve as a source of inspiration for China to march toward its great goals with confidence, unity and resolve. ■

item.title: Xi congratulates Central Institute of Socialism on 70th founding anniversary
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20
BEIJING, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday sent a congratulatory letter to the Central Institute of Socialism, celebrating its 70th founding anniversary. In the letter, Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, praised the institute for training a large number of non-CPC representatives who share the CPC's ideals and work in unity toward common goals, and for making important contributions to consolidating and developing the patriotic united front over the past 70 years. He encouraged the institute to continue strengthening political training, building broad political consensus, and improving the quality of its teaching and research as well as its governance capacity. Xi called on the institute to play a greater role in training talent for the united front, conducting theoretical research and promoting principles and policies, so as to better serve the overall work of the CPC and the country. The congratulatory letter was read out at a gathering marking the institute's anniversary in Beijing on Tuesday. Wang Huning, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, addressed the event. Wang said Xi's congratulatory message fully recognized the institute's achievements and contributions, and set out directions and requirements for strengthening the institute and enhancing its role. Wang said the CPC Central Committee has consistently supported the development of the institute over the past 70 years. He called for stronger political consensus-building through sustained political training, higher-quality education to better train personnel for the united front, and continued efforts to enforce strict management of the institute. The institute was established on Oct. 15, 1956.
